A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
provenance
The origin and history of evidence.
preliminary
Done before a fuller examination.
corroboration
Independent support for a claim.
attribution
Identification of a source in reporting.
second-hand
Learned from someone rather than witnessed.
evidential
Related to what facts can be established by proof.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Emma reached the newsroom early with a question that was ethical before it was investigative: what, exactly, had the correspondent consented to? A willingness to speak did not imply consent to recording, identification or publication. The person who had answered the invitation had agreed to speak privately, but had specifically asked that nobody record the conversation before discussing it. Emma checked with Sarah that a quiet meeting room was available.

The visitor introduced herself as Helen Ward. She said she had helped her younger cousin apply for travel support in 2011. Before saying anything about the application, she asked what the newspaper would do with her name.

Emma proposed a preliminary conversation without recording, explained the distinction between internal notes and publishable attribution, and asked Helen to decide which details could be retained. She would not publish identifying information without a further agreement. She also said she could not promise protection in every possible legal circumstance. Helen considered the limits, requested that her cousin remain unidentified, and agreed to proceed on those terms.

“I kept some of the papers,” Helen said. She opened a folder containing a photocopy of a completed application and a letter bearing the foundation's name. Emma distinguished the date printed on the photocopied letter from its unknown delivery date. Even an apparently official document required provenance checks before it could establish an event.

“The student was my cousin,” Helen explained. “I helped with the form. I don't want you to contact them without asking me first.”

Emma said she would not seek out the cousin through private records. She asked Helen to describe only what she knew first-hand. Helen's memory of helping complete the form was relatively clear. Her knowledge of receipt, however, was second-hand or uncertain; she could not remember witnessing the decision letter arrive.

Sarah had joined the meeting after Helen agreed. She asked whether the cousin had been rejected. Helen shook her head.

“I don't want to guess. We should read the letter properly. I haven't looked at it in years.”

Emma resisted the urge to capture either page. Permission to inspect a document was not permission to reproduce its personal details. She asked whether Helen would allow a later examination of copies with private details covered. Helen said she wanted to speak to her cousin first.

After the visitor left, Emma wrote a careful account of the conversation. The visitor's stated identity and relationship to the applicant remained claims awaiting independent confirmation. The documents had potential evidential value but neither their authenticity nor completeness had been checked, and Emma had not read the decision or established whether any grant had been paid.

Sarah seemed disappointed. “We finally meet someone, and we still don't have an answer.”

“We have a possible way to check,” Emma replied. “That matters more.”

She placed the notes in a private folder. For the first time, the investigation had moved from anonymous archive labels to a conversation with someone willing to discuss a real application. Whether the papers would support Helen's memories was the next question.
